stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy clearing expired stock offers it in three directions: to a licensed reverse distributor, to a volunteer overseas aid group that is not licensed to receive drugs, and to one of its own technicians who wants it for training purposes. Which of the transfers may lawfully proceed?

choices.text: All three, because expired stock is no longer a dispensable medicine at all.
All three, provided each recipient is told that the product has expired.
The transfer to the licensed reverse distributor, and neither of the other two.
The transfers to the reverse distributor and the aid group, but not the third.
None of them, because expired stock may never leave the pharmacy's custody.

explanation.core_reasoning: 247 CMR 9.01(12) bars a licensee from dispensing or distributing expired, outdated, defective, contaminated, counterfeit, contraband or otherwise substandard product to any person or entity who is NOT LICENSED OR LEGALLY AUTHORIZED TO RECEIVE it. The test is the recipient's authorisation, not the purpose of the transfer, so only the licensed reverse distributor qualifies.

choice_analysis.A: Expiry does not remove the product from the regulation; it is what brings it in.
choice_analysis.B: Disclosure is not a cure for an unauthorised recipient.
choice_analysis.C: Correct: only the licensed reverse distributor is an authorised recipient.
choice_analysis.D: A volunteer aid group that is not licensed cannot receive it.
choice_analysis.E: Transfer to an authorised recipient is permitted.

related_facts: Employment by the pharmacy does not make a technician an authorised recipient
explanation.mpje_trap: Candidates sort the transfers by how worthy the purpose looks rather than by the recipient's status.

reasoning_steps: Identify the product as within the listed substandard categories
Assess each proposed recipient for licensure or legal authorisation
Set aside the purpose of each transfer as irrelevant to the test
